newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland in mourning as rain threatens new floods.
newsitem.headline: Poland in mourning as rain threatens new floods.

text.p: Steady rain threatened a new wave of flooding on Friday as Poland mourned for its 48 dead and hundreds of communities struck by raging waters in the past two weeks.
"It is raining, from Koszalin (in the north) through all of western Poland, with varying intensity," flood crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes said.
"The situation doesn't look good," he told Reuters at 1230 GMT, after several hours of rain in southwestern areas.
Although the rains were were not as heavy as in the past, soaked ground and swollen rivers could not absorb the water.
Much depended on whether most of the rain fell in the west, where it would be troublesome, or in the south around the Czech border where long, heavy falls could be disastrous.
Flags were at half mast on Friday, churches held services and public broadcasters played serious music to mark a day of mourning.

Parliament during the night passed more than 20 bills allowing the government to increase borrowing and to rush both funds and aid to smitten areas. In the early hours, President Aleksander Kwasniewski announced he had signed them into law.
The parliament also hastily amended the communist-era state of emergency law, cutting its most undemocratic provisions, so it could be applied in case of a new round of the calamity.

President Kwasniewski supported the prime minister in opposing opposition calls to declare a state of emergency now in hard-hit regions, arguing that this would delay September 21 parliamentary elections and was unnecessary.

"But if it turns out that tomorrow or the next day we are dealing with a serious threat to very many provinces of Poland, we will have no alternative, we will have to take the decision," Kwasniewski said.

Poland's central bank rushed to the aid of the zloty, repeatedly selling dollars, as speculators drove the currency lower and foreign investors pulled out amid fears that flood relief measures would harm Poland's finances.
The bank's defence proved effective and the zloty closed slightly higher against a basket of foreign currencies.
In the neighbouring Czech Republic, where at least 46 people have died, foreboding gripped the country after forecasters also predicted heavy rain.
Learning lessons from the initial catastrophe, Poland's government deployed more than 20,000 troops to help with flood defences and set up a special communications network.

Among the spate of new laws were a relaxation of limits in this year's budget to give room for 2.5 billion zlotys ($714 million) of extra government borrowing from the central bank and a $300 million soft loan from the World Bank.

But high finance was far from the minds of exhausted people who faced a repeat of the nightmare that swamped more than 4,000 sq km of land and 970 towns and villages, leaving a shroud of filth and the danger of disease in its wake.
The current floods starting early last week inundated the south and then sent great swells northwards along the Wisla and Odra rivers, drowning the city streets of Wroclaw and Opole.
As new rain loomed, the Odra wave was moving towards the German border, prompting evacuations in parts of the Polish frontier town of Slubice which expected to be hit on Saturday.

Opposition parliamentarians, critical of the government's crisis management and scenting blood before the polls, kept up their attacks even while cooperating to get the urgent bills through parliament.
